title: Thursday's $3T tech sell-off, and what it means if you build AI products
content:
Market note · AI infrastructure
The $3 trillion ThursdayThursday's tech sell-off, and what it means if you build AI products
The Nasdaq fell 5.5 percent and chip stocks about 11 percent after voters turned against data centres. What happened, why it happened, the best and worst cases from here, and what I am changing in my own plans.
Closing tape · Thursday 5 November 2026
Closing levels for the S&P 500, Nasdaq and Dow; the rest are late-session readings. 4:00 p.m. ET close, Thursday 5 November 2026. Sources: CNBC, Yahoo Finance, Seeking Alpha.
The short version
Why did tech stocks fall on 5 November 2026? The Nasdaq Composite fell 5.5 percent and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index about 11 percent, the worst day for both since the tariff crash of April 2025, after Tuesday’s midterms gave Democrats both chambers of Congress and voters in ten states rejected most of the local data-centre measures on their ballots. Investors read that as a cap on the US AI build-out, and the selling hit a market that was already uneasy about AI capital spending outrunning cash flow, distressed-level credit at GPU cloud providers and 10-year Treasury yields near 5 percent.
Six minutes after the opening bell this morning, the Nasdaq had given back everything it gained in yesterday’s post-election rally. By the 4 p.m. close it was down 5.5 percent, its worst day since the tariff crash of April 2025, and it now sits in a correction, about 12 percent below the record it set on 6 October. More than $3 trillion of market value had left the index by midday, on Fortune’s count, and it closed lower than that.
I run product and engineering at an AI company. We rent compute, we sell AI software to large enterprises, and I spend a good part of my week with buyers and investors, so I read today’s tech sell-off with all three hats on. My read is that the market repriced the money and the concrete behind the AI build-out today, while the evidence on demand for AI did not move, and in one case got stronger.
Below is what happened, what caused it, the best, middle and worst cases from here with the odds I would put on each, and what I am changing in my own plans. Everything is as of Thursday evening, US Eastern time, and I have marked the numbers that are still being confirmed.
The damage
The chip index fell 11 percent and the companies that own AI capacity barely moved
Every one of the S&P 500’s eleven sectors closed lower, and by mid-afternoon 419 stocks in the index were down against 84 up. The Dow lost more than 1,800 points, its worst second session after a midterm election in records going back to 1896, and the Russell 2000 small-cap index joined the Nasdaq in correction territory. The VIX, the market’s fear gauge, jumped more than 60 percent to around 27.
The damage was lopsided in a way that matters. Nvidia fell about 9 percent and is back below where it ended last year. AMD and Micron lost about 15 percent each, Broadcom about 10 percent and Arm about 12 percent. CoreWeave, which borrows to build GPU capacity and rents it out, fell about 9 percent on top of Wednesday’s drop, roughly 18 percent in two days. Meanwhile Alphabet slipped 1.6 percent, Microsoft 2.8 percent and Meta 3.4 percent.
The market sold the companies that build and finance AI capacity much harder than the companies that own it. One way to read that, which several strategists made on Thursday, is that if new capacity gets harder to build, the capacity that already exists becomes more valuable.
On the $3 trillion figure doing the rounds tonight: it is for one session, and the count depends on which index you use. Fortune put the Nasdaq’s loss at more than $3 trillion at midday, when the index was down 5.2 percent, and the close was worse. Russia’s economy produces about $2.9 trillion a year on the IMF’s latest estimate, so the comparison people are making on X tonight holds, narrowly. I will update this paragraph when the closing tally is published.
Retail investors, who bought every dip for two years, sold. Vanda Research counted $358 million of net selling in individual stocks by 3 p.m., on track for the biggest retail selling day since 17 March 2020, and called it “a total capitulation by retail investors”.
The trigger
The trigger was the ballot box, and the target was the data centre
Tuesday’s midterms gave Democrats both chambers of Congress. On its own that did not frighten anyone; the Dow rose 1,569 points on Wednesday. What changed the maths for AI was what happened lower down the ballot.
Voters in ten states faced close to 40 local measures on data centres, and by Capital B’s count 77 percent of them voted against development. Forbes’s list runs to 41 measures, with Ohio alone passing 13 outright bans, and depending on how you count, between one and four local votes went the industry’s way. Ohio’s governor-elect, Amy Acton, campaigned on a conditional moratorium on new data centres unless they cover their full utility costs, and Georgia’s Keisha Lance Bottoms backed a pause on new construction. Texas, where a large share of the planned capacity was meant to go, had already paused permitting in September.
The industry heard it. Meta’s president, Dina Powell McCormick, said on Thursday that building data centres in the US is “going to be harder” and that hyperscalers are weighing whether to build outside the United States. Dan Ives of Yorkville, one of the loudest AI bulls on the street, now expects capital spending growth to peak next year instead of 2028 or 2029, and estimates that “on the low end 10% of the planned 800-1,000 AI focused data centers in the US will now be wiped off the roadmap”.
If your 2027 revenue depends on sites that may never be permitted, you got repriced today. That describes memory makers, power-equipment makers and the GPU clouds that borrowed against future capacity, and that is exactly the list of stocks that fell hardest.
The set-up
The market was already fragile because AI spending has outrun cash flow
A political headline cannot take 5 percent off the Nasdaq by itself. It needs a market that was already looking for a reason to sell, and October supplied three.
- Mon 6 OctNasdaq Composite closes at a record 27,599.89, the peak this correction is measured from.
- Wed 7 OctThe 10-year Treasury yield trades above 5.35 percent, its highest since 2002.
- Thu 8 OctReports put OpenAI’s annualised revenue around $50 billion, well below earlier figures. Nvidia, Oracle and CoreWeave fall.
- Thu 15 OctCoreWeave’s default insurance trades above 1,100 basis points, a distressed level. Oracle’s hits a record.
- Wed 28 OctThe Fed holds at 3.75 to 4.00 percent, with two members voting for another increase.
- Thu 29 OctAlphabet falls about 13 percent, its worst day on record, after reporting negative free cash flow and keeping 2026 spending at $195 to $205 billion.
- Fri 30 OctAmazon reports negative free cash flow on about $220 billion of spending. The Nasdaq ends its worst month since March 2025.
- Tue 3 NovElection day. After the close, AMD guides above expectations and says demand still exceeds supply.
- Wed 4 NovDemocrats win both chambers. The Dow rises 1,569 points. Underneath, Nvidia and CoreWeave already fall.
- Thu 5 NovThe Nasdaq erases its post-election gain in six minutes and closes down 5.5 percent.
The first reason is cash flow. In the earnings season that ended last week, Amazon, Alphabet and Meta all reported negative free cash flow, which is the cash a business has left after paying for its operations and its building programme. Amazon’s figure was minus $42 billion, Alphabet’s minus $9 billion and Meta’s minus $2 billion, and Microsoft’s free cash flow fell 27 percent to $19 billion, with a plan to go to the bond market for more. Alphabet lost about $500 billion of value in a single day on 29 October for keeping its spending guidance at $195 to $205 billion. BlackRock’s numbers show why investors flinched. report.summary: A political backlash to data centers and fragile AI capex sent the Nasdaq down 5.5% and chips 11%, erasing over $3 trillion in one session.
report.background: The sell-off followed Tuesday's US midterms, which gave Democrats both chambers of Congress and saw voters in ten states reject most local data-center measures. Investors read that as a cap on the US AI build-out. The market was already fragile: hyperscalers are reporting negative free cash flow as AI capital spending outruns cash generation, GPU cloud providers show distressed credit, and 10-year Treasury yields are near 5%. The article argues the market repriced the money and concrete behind AI infrastructure, while evidence on AI demand did not weaken.
key_points: The Nasdaq fell 5.5% and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index about 11%, their worst day since April 2025. More than $3 trillion of market value left the Nasdaq by midday, and the index entered a correction roughly 12% below its October record.

The trigger was lower-ballot politics: about 77% of nearly 40 local data-center measures in ten states were rejected, with Ohio passing 13 outright bans. Texas had already paused permitting in September, and politicians in Ohio and Georgia backed moratoriums or pauses.

The market sold AI-capacity builders and financiers harder than AI-capacity owners. Nvidia fell about 9%, AMD and Micron about 15% each, and CoreWeave about 18% in two days, while Alphabet, Microsoft and Meta fell much less. Existing capacity may become more valuable if new builds are blocked.

The setup was already weak. Amazon, Alphabet and Meta reported negative free cash flow, Microsoft's free cash flow fell 27%, and CoreWeave's default insurance traded at distressed levels. Retail investors also sold heavily, which Vanda called a total capitulation.

The author's read is that demand for AI did not move while the cost and feasibility of building US capacity did. Dan Ives expects capex growth to peak earlier and estimates at least 10% of planned US AI data centers may be wiped from the roadmap.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the sell-off signals that US data-center permitting and local politics are now material investment risks, not just power or chip constraints. Capex growth may peak earlier, and planned capacity could be delayed or moved abroad. Developers may face tighter or pricier GPU capacity, especially from borrowed-against-future-capacity cloud providers, while owners of existing capacity gain leverage. Enterprises could slow procurement as vendors reassess roadmaps. For regular users, the near-term effect is less about AI demand disappearing and more about supply growth slowing, which could keep prices firmer and delay new products that depend on fresh compute.
report.tools: To track the signal, watch grid interconnection queues and open energy data via GridStatus.io and EIA-860, local permitting trackers and data-center maps such as Data Center Map and OpenStreetMap, GPU cloud price and availability trackers such as Vast.ai and Genesis Cloud, plus credit indicators like CoreWeave CDS and hyperscaler free-cash-flow reports.
